title: Adding a URL Made My Writing 49% More Human
author: Jacob Carr
source: What Teachers Have to Say (whatteachershavetosay.substack.com), November 16, 2026
summary: Carr uses a Palo Alto case in which Turnitin flagged a sophomore's essay as 76 percent AI, the student rewrote it in class, received a D and the family's 1,162 pages of evidence changed nothing, to argue that detector scores are a poor foundation for cheating findings. He pairs it with his own survey in which 640 educators split 50.2 to 49.8 on whether a student who outlines, has AI draft and then edits is cheating, showing that teachers have no settled professional judgement for a court or district to defer to. His core point is that accuracy is the smaller problem, since a probability score cannot be rebutted by any evidence a student can produce. He tests Substack's own detector, where a 2015 essay scored 100 percent AI and adding a link changed a score without altering a word. For leaders he proposes asking what they would have done without the score, treating it only as a preliminary signal, publishing rebuttal criteria in advance and declaring permitted AI use per task with the AI Assessment Scale.
points: A detector score is not rebuttable, because nothing a student produces changes the number and the method is undisclosed.
Educators genuinely disagree about the middle cases of AI use, so consequences currently depend on which teacher a student has.
Ask what you would have done without the score; if you would not have investigated, the detector is raising suspicion your own judgement did not.
Use the score at most as a signal that starts a look at drafts, revision history and a conversation, never as a finding or a trigger for consequences.
Declare in advance the level of AI use each task allows and publish how a student can rebut a concern.
quotes: The room splits, and not gently. Teachers at the same table, sometimes teaching the same course, land on opposite sides and then look at each other with gut-level surprise.

As of this fall, 640 educators have answered that outline question, and 50.2 percent lean more toward the cheating side while 49.8 percent land on the other. Six hundred and forty professionals, and the result is a coin flip.

Deference assumes there’s a settled professional judgment to defer to, while my own experience with educators say there isn’t one, which means the consequence a student gets depends on which room they walked into in August and navigating unclear rules.
But, a probability score can’t clear anybody, because there’s nothing a student can produce that changes the number, and the algorithm used to find it isn’t even disclosed.
I pasted the URL at the bottom and ran it again: 51 percent AI, 49 percent human. I didn’t change a single word I’d written.

If you’re a leader deciding whether to keep a detector switched on, start with one question: what would you have done without the score? If you’d have looked into it anyway, because the writing didn’t sound like the kid you heard in class last week, the number adds very little.
if you use one at all, treat the score as a preliminary signal, never as proof. What makes it a signal and not a verdict is everything that happens after it.
The AI Assessment Scale lets a teacher declare, ahead of time, what level of AI use a task allows, so a concern later is measured against something the student actually saw.
